Project 1 — Wind Speed Prediction Using Weather Data (STATS 101A)

← 한국어 버전

How Much Can Weather Data Explain Wind Speed?

This project examined how much changes in wind speed could be explained using commonly available weather information such as Temperature, Humidity, Visibility, and Pressure.

Using weather data from Szeged, Hungary, between 2006 and 2016, we built and compared several regression models to identify which weather factors were meaningfully related to wind speed.

Project Overview

The analysis used Wind Speed as the outcome and the following four meteorological variables:

  • Temperature
  • Humidity
  • Visibility
  • Pressure

We first built a multiple linear regression model using all four variables.

We then examined whether each variable meaningfully contributed to explaining wind speed, compared the full model with a simpler model, and evaluated both the explanatory power and statistical limitations of the final model.

My Role

I was responsible for topic selection, data preprocessing, statistical analysis, and final report writing.

I prepared the dataset, built and interpreted the multiple linear regression models, and documented the model comparisons, diagnostic results, and limitations in the final report.

Analysis Approach

1. Building a model with all four weather variables

We first built a multiple linear regression model using Temperature, Humidity, Visibility, and Pressure.

In the full model, Temperature, Humidity, and Pressure showed statistically significant relationships with wind speed, while Visibility did not.

2. Determining whether Visibility was necessary

To determine whether Visibility was necessary in the model, we compared a model that included Visibility with one that excluded it.

The Partial F-test produced a p-value of 0.6459, suggesting that removing Visibility did not significantly reduce the explanatory power of the model.

We therefore selected the reduced model using:

Temperature · Humidity · Pressure

3. Evaluating the model

After selecting the final model, we examined residual plots and additional diagnostic measures to determine whether the assumptions of the regression model were reasonable.

We also calculated the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) to check whether the predictor variables contained excessive overlapping information.

Key Findings

The final model used:

Temperature · Humidity · Pressure

The model explained approximately 18% of the variation in wind speed.

This suggested that the selected weather variables were related to wind speed, but they were not sufficient to explain most of its variation.

The final regression equation was:

Wind Speed = 282.486
− 0.295(Temperature)
− 17.426(Humidity)
− 0.251(Pressure)

Model Diagnostics

The residuals generally did not show a strong systematic pattern, although their spread increased in some regions with higher fitted values.

A Breusch–Pagan test also produced a very small p-value, indicating that heteroscedasticity, or non-constant residual variance, remained a limitation of the model.

In contrast, all VIF values were below 2, suggesting that severe multicollinearity was not a concern.

The Residuals vs. Leverage plot also did not indicate any clearly influential observations that substantially distorted the model.

Exploring an Alternative Model

We also examined whether a Box-Cox transformation could improve the model.

However, the transformed model produced a slightly lower Adjusted R² and introduced additional deviation in part of the Q-Q plot.

Because the transformation increased model complexity without providing a meaningful improvement, we retained the untransformed reduced model.

Limitations

This project also demonstrated that identifying statistically meaningful relationships is different from achieving strong predictive performance.

Only a limited set of weather variables was included in the analysis.

Date information was not incorporated into the model, preventing us from accounting for seasonal patterns in wind speed.

Other potentially relevant variables, such as Wind Bearing, were also excluded.

Therefore, the relatively low R² of approximately 0.18 suggests that much of the variation in wind speed may be influenced by factors not included in the model.

Methods Used

  • Multiple Linear Regression
  • Full Model / Reduced Model Comparison
  • Partial F-test
  • Residual Diagnostics
  • Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
  • Breusch–Pagan Test
  • Box-Cox Transformation
